steps.description: Conduct a parameter sweep on small ReLU feedforward networks to measure the minimum hidden layer width N_c(w) required to achieve zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3 on 20 held-out constraint points) as the number of training constraints w increases from 10 to 200. Design the experiment with the following steps: (1) Construct the constraint function f(x) = sin(πx) on [0,1] with w training points (plus noise σ=1e-4) and 20 held-out test points; (2) Train networks with hidden widths w_h ∈ {8,16,32,64,128,256} using Adam (lr=1e-3, max 10k iterations, early stopping); (3) Record the smallest width achieving zero violation for each w; (4) Repeat 5 times and average; (5) Plot N_c(w) vs w to determine if the solution space is rigid (N_c bounded ≤64) or fat (N_c unbounded or fails to converge). SKILL: None (custom exploration)

Implement a numerical experiment to measure the solution space rigidity of small ReLU feedforward networks. Train networks with hidden widths w_h ∈ {8,16,32,64,128,256} using Adam (lr=1e-3, 10k max iters, early stopping). Record the minimum width N_c(w) achieving zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3 on 20 held-out points). Execute 5 independent runs per w and report the trend of N_c(w) to determine rigidity (bounded N_c ≤ 64) vs fatness (N_c unbounded).

steps.description: Conduct a numerical experiment to test the hypothesis that the solution space is rigid due to low-rank constraints by measuring N_c(w) (minimum hidden layer width achieving zero violation on held-out constraints) as a function of constraint count w. Steps: (1) Construct a 1D function approximation problem with w constraint points (sin(πx) on [0,1] with Gaussian noise σ=1e-4); (2) Train small ReLU feedforward networks with hidden widths w_h ∈ {8,16,32,64,128,256} using Adam (lr=1e-3, max 10k iterations, early stopping); (3) Evaluate zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on 20 held-out points; (4) Record N_c(w) as the smallest width achieving zero violation for each w ∈ {10,20,50,100,200}; (5) Repeat 5 times and average results. This directly tests whether N_c(w) stays constant at 16 (rigid) or grows (fat).

Reformulate the solution space rigidity hypothesis within [DIM: geometry] by testing geometric constraints on manifolds. Construct three geometric constraint sets: (1) point-set registration on S^2 (interpolation of 10-200 points on a unit sphere with geodesic error ≤ 1e-3), (2) Laplace-Beltrami residual constraints on embedded manifolds (solving Δu = f on S^2 with L2 error ≤ 1e-3), and (3) conformal mapping constraints (preserving angles on Riemann surfaces). Sweep hidden widths w_h ∈ {8,16,32,64,128,256} and constraint counts w ∈ {10,20,50,100,200}, measuring N_c(w) as the minimum width achieving geometric zero violation (geodesic/angular error ≤ 1e-3). Use ReLU networks, Adam (lr=1e-3), 10k iterations with early stopping, 5 repeats per (w,w_h). If N_c(w) ≤ 64 across all w, geometric rigidity is proven; if all w_h fail on geometric constraints, classify as "fat".

Design and execute a numerical experiment to measure the solution space rigidity of small ReLU feedforward networks. Define "rigidity" as the existence of a finite, bounded minimum network width N_c(w) (≤64) that achieves zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on w held-out constraint points, without N_c(w) growing with w. Construct a set of analytical constraints (e.g., polynomial interpolation or PDE residual constraints), train networks with varying hidden widths (8–256), and compute N_c(w) as a function of constraint count w (10–200). Use 5 random repeats for statistical significance. If N_c(w) stays bounded, rigidity is achieved; if all widths fail up to 256, the space is "fat".

Design and execute a numerical experiment to test the Stochastic Regularization Hypothesis regarding solution space rigidity in small feedforward networks. Specifically, we will: (1) construct a set of analytic constraints (e.g., polynomial interpolation or PDE residual constraints); (2) train small ReLU feedforward networks with hidden widths scanned from 8 to 256; (3) evaluate zero-violation (max abs error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out constraint points as a function of constraint count w (10 to 200); (4) compute N_c(w) = minimum width achieving zero violation; (5) assess whether N_c(w) remains bounded (≤64) as w increases, indicating rigidity, or grows unbounded, indicating fatness. This directly tests the core hypothesis using the defined metric.

The hypothesis concerns differential equation residual rigidity in small feedforward networks. I will create a Python script that: (1) constructs a 1D Poisson differential equation residual constraint system (-u'' = f with boundary conditions), (2) trains small ReLU feedforward networks with varying hidden widths (8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256) on w constraint points (10, 20, 50, 100, 200), (3) measures zero-violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on held-out points, and (4) computes N_c(w) to determine if the solution space is rigid (N_c bounded ≤ 64) or fat (N_c unattainable). The script will implement the physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach to enforce differential equation residuals directly in the loss function.

Design and run a systematic scan of small ReLU feedforward networks to measure the minimal hidden layer width N_c(w) required to achieve zero violation (max absolute error ≤ 1e-3) on out-of-sample constraints as the number of constraints w increases from 10 to 200. We will test on two constraint types: (1) point-wise interpolation of f(x)=sin(πx) on [0,1], and (2) residual constraints of the Poisson equation -u''=f. The goal is to determine whether N_c(w) remains bounded (≤64, indicating rigidity) or grows unbounded (indicating "fat" solution space). We will run 5 repetitions per (w, w_h) pair and report mean N_c(w) with standard deviation.
